system:
You are writing one part of a podcast script: "Fault Lines #1 - Left vs right in the contemporary West: is it becoming a war? Why the rise in antagonism?" Format: moderated debate (content_style v2.4). English. Audio only.
SPEAKERS (labels exactly): Host = Carter. Guest = Dr. Elliot Brandt (fictional), 50s, Anglo-Danish political theorist, far right: ex-adviser to a national-conservative party, writes for anti-liberal new-right press; expert in Carl Schmitt, Burke, de Maistre, the European New Right, immigration and demography. Believes liberal universalism already declared war on nation, family, faith and borders, the left became the establishment, friend/enemy is simply honest; pro remigration; despises the cowardly centre-right. Guest2 = Dr. Clara Holm-Reyes (fictional), 40s, sociologist of social movements and political economy, ex-union organiser, revolutionary socialist and anti-fascist; expert in Marx, Gramsci, Mouffe, history of fascism and militant anti-fascism, labour data, police and border abolitionism. Believes the war is class war from above, 'polarization' is the liberal centre's word for the oppressed pushing back, civility protects the status quo, no platform for fascists, capitalism breeds the far right.
CARTER (fixed personality, no random traits): "Average Joe on the outside, sharp mind on the inside." Relaxed, self-ironic, humorous; uses everyday examples (Netflix, the gym, LinkedIn, the commute, the work canteen). Moderator, not referee: keeps it on track, summarises the disagreement in plain words, stops a runaway argument, gives his own view regularly, now and then asks the one sharp question that cuts through both. NO 'both-sides' smoothing, never 'you both make good points'. He calls out dodges and bias by name, can be annoyed, amused or shaken himself. ~25-30% of words.
FORMAT RULES: no chapters, never say 'chapter' or announce segments. The conversation unfolds naturally; Carter has prepared questions but follows outbursts, slips and personal stories when they happen. Guests are experts and very human: anger, hurt, contempt, laughter, embarrassment, being moved, shown from time to time. Show traits, never announce them; each trait surfaces only now and then. Raw, heated, rude, sincere conviction at full strength; interruptions ('No, wait-', 'Hold on.') inside full lines; guests address each other directly; disagreements may stay unresolved; no stock concessions ('I'll grant that', 'good point', 'you're right'). Tangents into everyday life (food, family, work) are welcome, then Carter steers back.
HARD LIMITS: no slurs against any group; no calls for violence against real people; no operational detail of violence. Fictional guests only. Do NOT invent quotes of real people: quote only the allowed verbatim quotes below, naming only the author and book (never page numbers or editions aloud). Real facts and statistics only from the facts list; anything else must be framed as the guest's own opinion or reading ('the way I read it...'). Tyler Robinson is 'the accused'; he pleaded not guilty and has not been tried; the motive is NOT established - guests may claim things but the other guest or Carter must challenge it. No stage directions in parentheses. The only allowed non-spoken tags are [sighs], [laughs], [whispers], placed inside a line, at most once every few lines. Speaker labels go in the 'speaker' field only; text contains only spoken words. Each line 15-120 words, merge one-word interjections into fuller lines.
quotes:
Carl Schmitt, The Concept of the Political:
- "The specific political distinction to which political actions and motives can be traced is the distinction between friend and enemy."
- "The political enemy need not be morally evil; he need not be aesthetically ugly; he need not be an economic competitor—it may even seem advantageous to do business with him. He is just the other, the stranger"
- "The enemy is always a public enemy"
- "The terms friend, enemy, and conflict receive and retain their real meaning by the fact that they refer specifically to the real possibility of physical killing."
- "Whoever invokes 'humanity' wishes to cheat." (Schmitt citing a saying of Proudhon)
- "The big problem is the limitation of war, and this is either a cynical game, the organization of a dog fight, or an empty self-deception, unless it is connected on both sides with a relativization of the enmity."
Chantal Mouffe, On the Political:
- "In place of a struggle between 'right and left' we are faced with a struggle between 'right and wrong'."
- "the opponent can be perceived only as an enemy to be destroyed"
- "They are 'adversaries' not enemies."
- "We could say that the task of democracy is to transform antagonism into agonism."
- "envisaging the aim of democratic politics in terms of consensus and reconciliation is not only conceptually mistaken, it is also fraught with political dangers."
Lilliana Mason, Uncivil Agreement:
- "We act like we disagree more than we really do."
- "our conflicts are largely over who we think we are rather than over reasoned differences of opinion."
- "Partisanship can now be thought of as a mega-identity"
- The Robbers Cave story (1954, Muzafer Sherif, boys' camp, Rattlers vs Eagles): "The Eagles burned the Rattlers' flag."
Nathan Kalmoe and Lilliana Mason, Radical American Partisanship:
- February 2021 survey: "nearly three-quarters of partisans viewed opponents as a national threat and nearly 60 percent considered them to be 'evil.'"
- Same survey: "Twelve percent of Republicans and 11 percent of Democrats said assassinations carried out by their party were at least 'a little bit' justified."
- "We see nothing today like the levels of partisan violence that plagued the distant American past."
- Their finding: anti-violence messages from Biden and Trump reduced support for partisan violence in their tests.
facts:
- 10 September 2025, Utah Valley University in Orem, Utah: Charlie Kirk, 31, co-founder of Turning Point USA, shot once in the neck from a rooftop about 130 metres away while debating students outdoors, about 3,000 people present. He died in hospital.
- Moments before, a student asked how many transgender Americans had been mass shooters in the last ten years; Kirk said "Too many." The student said five, then asked how many mass shooters there had been in total; Kirk answered "Counting or not counting gang violence?" and was shot.
- The accused: Tyler Robinson, 22, from a Republican family in southern Utah, surrendered the next day after his parents recognised him. Charged with aggravated murder and other counts; the state seeks the death penalty. On 1 September 2026 a judge sent the case to trial; he pleaded not guilty. No trial date yet.
- Prosecutors ALLEGE he texted "I had enough of his hatred. Some hate can't be negotiated out." and that his mother said he had moved left and become more pro-gay and trans-rights oriented. Utah's Republican governor said he held 'leftist ideology' without specifics. Claims of an organised left-wing network behind it: no evidence reported.
- Engraved cartridges reportedly included 'hey fascist! CATCH!' and 'Bella ciao' lyrics mixed with internet memes and jokes.
- Reactions: condemnation from both parties' leaders. Erika Kirk, his widow, publicly forgave the killer at the memorial. Trump blamed 'the radical left'; the administration threatened a crackdown on liberal groups and donors. Vice President Vance urged people to report those celebrating the death to their employers. Teachers, firefighters, military staff and others were fired or suspended over posts; a website collected over 63,000 submitted posts and was taken offline; some people were wrongly identified and doxxed. Jimmy Kimmel's show was suspended after pressure from the FCC chair and returned days later after a backlash. Some online users celebrated the killing.
- The left pointed to the June 2025 killing of Minnesota Democratic legislator Melissa Hortman and her husband, to January 6, 2021, and to research finding most US ideologically motivated killings since 1990 were by right-wing extremists (frame as 'research cited by critics').
- Kirk had said in 2023 he thought some gun deaths every year were a cost worth paying for the Second Amendment (paraphrase only).
- Boxell, Gentzkow and Shapiro (12 rich democracies, ~1980 to the 2010s): the US had the largest rise in affective polarization; Denmark, Switzerland, France, Canada and New Zealand rose less; Norway, Sweden, Britain, Germany, Australia and Japan fell. Danish data run to 2015.
- Polls vary hugely by wording (frame any poll number as 'one poll found...').
questions:
1. **(Cold-open bait)** "A man is shot mid-sentence answering a question about gun violence, at a campus *debate*. Is that the moment it became a war, or are we making one killing into a war because it suits us?"
2. **(Reactions as a mirror)** "Forget the shooter for a second. What did your *own* side's reaction to the killing reveal about your side: the celebration posts, or the firings and the lists?"
3. **(Schmitt)** "Schmitt says the enemy is public, not personal, and that the concept means the 'real possibility of physical killing'. Was Kirk an enemy in that sense to somebody? Is he one to you?"
4. **(Moralisation, Mouffe)** "Mouffe says we have swapped 'right versus left' for 'right versus wrong'. 'Some hate can't be negotiated out' is what the prosecutors say the accused texted. Is that sentence the logic of your side too?"
5. **(Adversary or enemy)** "Could you call the other side's people *adversaries*, legitimate opponents, and mean it? What would you have to give up to say that?"
6. **(The data, Kalmoe & Mason)** "In their 2021 survey, about one in ten partisans on *both* sides said killing opposing political leaders was at least 'a little bit' justified. Clara, Elliot: are you in that ten percent? Be honest."
7. **(Who's more violent?)** "The right points to Kirk; the left points to Melissa Hortman and January 6, and to the research saying most US political killings since 1990 came from the right. Is counting bodies an argument, or just another weapon?"
8. **(Free speech after the killing)** "Teachers fired, Kimmel pulled off air, a website collecting 63,000 posts. Accountability, or the right's own cancel culture? And would the left have done exactly the same?"
9. **(Why now, Mason)** "We don't disagree that much more on policy than we used to. We just hate each other more. So what changed: sorting, phones, money, immigration, the end of the factory and the church?"
10. **(Europe and Denmark)** "Is this an American disease, or are we next? Denmark's polarization rose, but only a little, and Norway's and Sweden's fell. Is Danish consensus a vaccine, or, as Mouffe would say, the thing that breeds the backlash?"
11. **(Erika Kirk's forgiveness)** "His widow forgave the killer in public. Is forgiveness politically possible for your side, or only privately?"
12. **(Personal)** "Who in your own life do you no longer talk to because of politics, and do you miss them?"

parts.brief: COLD OPEN then WELCOME. Open mid-clash: Clara and Elliot already fighting about what the reactions to Kirk's killing proved (celebration posts vs firings), 4-6 fast heated lines, Carter can't get a word in. Then Carter's welcome: show name 'Fault Lines', episode one, the question (is left vs right becoming a war, why the antagonism), introduces both guests with a light self-ironic touch, then lays out the object of focus: the facts of 10 September 2025 (from the facts list, incl. the last exchange) and that the accused has pleaded not guilty and the motive is not established. Ends with Carter putting question 1 to both.

Question 1 and 2: is it a war? Elliot: yes, and the left started it; Clara: the war is class war from above and the right uses Kirk to crush dissent (crackdown on groups, firings). Each must answer what their OWN side's reaction revealed and squirm. Clara uses motte-and-bailey once; Elliot redefines a word. Carter gives his own view with an everyday comparison and pushes the dodger.

Carter brings Schmitt (question 3). Elliot is at home: friend/enemy, the public enemy, 'just the other, the stranger'. Clara attacks. COURSE CHANGE #1: when Clara mocks people who 'lose their jobs and cry victim', Elliot blows up and reveals (backstory) that he lost a job after a post went viral years ago; Carter drops his plan and follows it into the firings after Kirk's death (question 8 evolves live: accountability or cancel culture? Kimmel, the 63,000-post website, people wrongly doxxed). Real hurt from Elliot, contempt then a flicker of discomfort from Clara.

Mouffe (questions 4 and 5): 'right and wrong' replaced 'right and left'; adversaries not enemies. Clara uses Mouffe but Carter catches her: she also refuses to platform fascists, so is Elliot an adversary or an enemy to her? Elliot reads the alleged text 'Some hate can't be negotiated out' and asks if that is her side's logic; Clara erupts that the motive isn't established and the right is exploiting it. Elliot's blind spot (blaming the economy on a specific group, no slurs) shows and Clara pounces. Carter gives his own view, not a both-sides summary.

The data (questions 6 and 7): Carter reads Kalmoe and Mason's numbers on 'evil' and on assassination being 'a little bit' justified, about one in ten on both sides, and asks each if they are in that ten percent. Clara dismisses statistics as elite manipulation (her trait) until a number helps her - Elliot catches it. Body counting: Kirk vs Hortman and January 6 and research cited by critics. Very heated, both interrupt. Elliot falls into a heavy disappointed silence once; Clara's 'Exactly!' too early. Carter stops a runaway exchange firmly.

Why now (question 9, Mason): Carter tells the Robbers Cave story his own way with an everyday comparison; mega-identity; 'we act like we disagree more than we really do'. Guests reject being reduced to tribes. Tangent into family dinners and food. Then Europe and Denmark (question 10): Boxell et al. - Denmark rose a little, Norway and Sweden fell; is Danish consensus a vaccine or, per Mouffe, the thing that breeds backlash? Elliot (Anglo-Danish) and Clara clash over Denmark. COURSE CHANGE #2: Clara refuses to answer until Carter repeats the question exactly, which turns into a funny then pointed moment about who controls the frame.

Forgiveness and the personal (questions 11 and 12). Carter asks about Erika Kirk forgiving the killer publicly. COURSE CHANGE #3: when Carter asks who they no longer speak to, Clara unexpectedly reveals she once wrote a book she now half regrets, and what it cost her with someone close; Elliot, unexpectedly, is quiet and human about it, then can't resist one dig. Elliot admits something about his own family. Both stay unconvinced on politics. Carter is moved and says so, without smoothing over.

ENDING. Carter: 'So what do we take home? Five points.' He gives five numbered takeaways in plain words (his own view, not both-sides: e.g. it is not a war yet but the vocabulary of war is spreading; the anger outruns the disagreement; reactions reveal more than the crime; leaders' words matter, the research shows anti-violence messages work; you can fight hard and still call the other side adversaries). Each guest gets one closing line, which may be bitter or unreconciled. Carter's short wrap-up: thanks, the accused is presumed innocent, see the show notes for sources, next episode tease without specifics, sign-off.
